text: This chapter is your capstone: pick a real combinatorial optimization problem, formulate it as a QUBO, build a hybrid quantum-classical workflow around it, benchmark it fairly against a classical baseline, and document the result honestly. This lesson walks through a fully worked model problem you'll use as your template.

A good capstone problem needs three properties. It's naturally expressible as binary variables with a quadratic or linear cost -- if you need cubic or higher terms, reformulate. It's small enough, roughly 4 to 10 variables, that you can brute-force verify the true optimum yourself. And it has a real-world interpretation you can explain in one or two sentences to someone outside this course. If your instinct is toward something bigger or more exotic, scope it down first.

Here's the model problem: four tasks, taking 3, 5, 2, and 4 hours, split between two workers, minimizing the squared imbalance in total hours. This is a direct instance of the classic Number Partitioning problem. Checking all 16 possible assignments directly: dumping everything on one worker gives an imbalance-squared of 196; a 6-8 split gives 4; but a 7-7 split, achieved two different ways, gives exactly 0 -- the true optimum, confirmed by brute force.

Number Partitioning's objective, expanded algebraically, is a pure QUBO -- the squared-difference structure produces exactly the quadratic interaction terms from Lesson 2, and it converts cleanly into Ising and Pauli-Z form using the same machinery as every other problem in this course. Before moving to Lesson 25, confirm you can state your own problem's decision variables, objective, and constraints in writing; that you can brute-force verify its true optimum; and that you have a specific classical baseline in mind.

Next lesson runs this model problem through the full pipeline -- QUBO, Ising Hamiltonian, and an actual simulated QAOA circuit -- including a genuinely surprising result that's worth sitting with rather than smoothing over.
